summary: Discovery focused on per-token economics and hosting options for a sandbox/pilot. Customer evaluating Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for a healthcare diagnostics assistant (PHI in some flows). Main concerns: token burn, latency SLOs, KV/prefix caching, pilot budget cap, and KMS/SSO for compliance. Agreed next steps: send pricing spreadsheet, run sandbox benchmark with sample prompt set, schedule security deep-dive.
transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone thanks for taking time, quick intro — I'm Sofia, AE on the inference team at Redwood. Ethan's my SE and he'll handle the benchmark and technical bits today.
[00:08] Priya: Hi Sofia, hey Ethan, thanks. I'm Priya, Head of ML at NebulaThera. Jon and Liam are here too.
[00:13] Jon: hi, thanks.
[00:15] Ethan: nice to meet you all. Can you give a bit of context on what you're trying to achieve with the sandbox/pilot?
[00:22] Priya: Yeah, so we're building a diagnostic assistant that ingests patient notes and returns a structured summary and risk flags. Some flows will have PHI, some not. Our goal is to validate latency and cost before committing. Budget for pilot is tight — roughly 8k USD for the month for inference.
[00:37] Jon: The SLO we're targeting for interactive sessions is p95 < 600ms for short prompts (under 512 tokens). Throughput won't be huge initially, maybe 50-100 reqs/minute.
[00:48] Sofia: Great — those are helpful targets. A few areas we usually dig into: per-token pricing expectations, batching and cache levers (we have prefix and KV-style caching), and whether Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private makes sense given residency and PHI needs.
[01:03] Liam: For PHI we'd prefer private or at least VPC-hosted control plane — we need KMS that integrates with our existing vault and full audit logs. SOC2 is a yes.
[01:12] Ethan: Understood. For the sandbox pilot, we can provision a private VPC-connected sandbox (not full on-prem) so you can test residency-like behaviour and KMS integration. It's quicker than a full Private deployment.
[01:23] Priya: Quick question on pricing — how does per-token change with batching and quantization? We're sensitive to burst costs.
[01:30] Sofia: Short answer: batching reduces per-token compute in many cases, especially for short prompts where fixed overheads dominate. Our pricing table for Hosted is per input+output token, and Dedicated offers reserved capacity pricing with a lower marginal per-token but with commit. Quantization affects throughput and can reduce cost by 20-50% depending on model and quant level.
[01:49] Jon: If we do Dedicated, what's the minimum commit? We don't want to overcommit given pilot.
[01:55] Sofia: For Dedicated we typically start with a monthly pool equivalent to one or two GPU nodes depending on model class. We can map a pilot-sized commit with an exit/scale window — we can propose a shorter trial contract. I'll include that in the sheet.
[02:06] [02:06] Priya: Can you explain KV cache vs prefix cache again? When is one preferable?
[02:11] Ethan: Sure. Prefix caching stores repeated prefixes so if you have long system prompts or repeated context we keep that in mem to avoid re-computation. KV cache is the attention key-value cache for autoregressive decoding — useful for multi-turn chat where you reuse context across steps. For your flows where we summarize long notes, prefix caching helps for common instruction frames, and KV caching reduces repeated decoder cost if you do streaming or multi-step generation.
[02:31] Priya: So if we do a chunked summarize of a 2k token note, would batching help?
[02:35] Ethan: Batching helps if you have many parallel users with smallish requests. For a single long request (2k tokens) batching isn't helpful, but prefix/KV optimizations and quantization/compilation kernels will. Also if you can split into smaller chunks and run those in parallel across requests, batching can amortize startup overhead.
[02:54] Jon: Any gotchas with latency when quantizing? We need p95.
[02:59] Ethan: Lower precision sometimes increases throughput but can add slight variance in kernel selection. For p95, we recommend testing the quant profile in the sandbox — often q4/q5 gives near-native latency with big cost savings, but results vary by model.
[03:13] Liam: For the KMS requirement, we use HashiCorp Vault with an HSM-backed cluster — can Redwood integrate?
[03:19] Sofia: Yes — we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integration for Private and can do VPC/KMS in the sandbox for evaluation. We'll surface the integration details in the security follow-up doc.
[03:30] [03:30] Priya: ok, what about token accounting — do you count tokens before reranking calls and embeddings? We have a rerank-heavy flow.
[03:38] Ethan: We count per request including reranker calls. For embeddings we bill per embedding unit; reranks that make additional generation calls are charged for those tokens. For reranking use case it's often cheaper to use specialized short-sequence models or server-side caching of candidate embeddings to reduce token calls.
[03:56] Jon: Should we consider ghosting some steps to reduce burn? Like do partial caching or store intermediate embeddings?
[04:02] Ethan: Exactly. Cache embeddings for static candidate sets, use prefix caching for standard instruction frames, and apply result-level caching for identical prompts. All reduce marginal token spend.
[04:12] Priya: On the pilot budget — with 8k, any rough estimate on how many sessions we can run if average session uses 400 tokens output + 200 input?
[04:20] Sofia: Rough back-of-envelope: at Hosted list rates for a mid-sized open model, that might be ~0.0007 USD per token (example) — so 600 tokens ~ 0.42 USD per session, that's about ~19k sessions for 8k. But real numbers depend on batching, caching and whether you use Dedicated (lower marginal). We'll send a modeled sheet with sensitivity to batch rate, cache hit, and quantization (we'll include q4 scenario).
[04:44] Jon: That helps. Also concerned about throughput—if we scale to 300 req/min later how does autoscale and burst capacity work?
[04:52] Sofia: Dedicated provides predictable throughput with reserved GPU pool and burst options. Hosted autoscaling handles spikes but with less SLA predictability. We can model throughput vs cost — the spawned sheet will show cost at different RPS and cache-hit assumptions.
[05:06] Priya: For the sandbox run can we instrument token-level traces and latency per model variant? We want to compare 13B vs 70B-ish family.
[05:14] Ethan: Yes — sandbox telemetry will include token-level cost breakdown, per-request latency histograms, and we can add per-model dashboards. We'll need your prompt sets and sample loads to run that.
[05:24] Liam: One more — audit logs and retention: we need 12 months of audit for certain actions. Is that supported?
[05:30] Sofia: For Private we can configure retention and export to your SIEM. Hosted has log retention tiers; we can add an add-on for extended retention. We'll capture requirements in the security doc.
[05:41] [05:41] Jon: Are there any compliance limitations we should know about re: PHI in Hosted?
[05:45] Sofia: Hosted can support certain compliance use cases but for PHI we usually recommend Private or at least Dedicated with VPC + KMS so you control keys and residency. We'll outline tradeoffs in the security follow-up.
[05:58] Priya: Ok, next steps from our side: we'll share a 500-prompt sample, and Liam will send KMS vendor details.
[06:06] Sofia: Perfect. We'll send the sandbox pricing and pilot modeler, and Ethan will reach out to schedule the benchmark. Any other questions?
[06:14] Priya: Not right now. Thanks.
[06:16] Jon: Thanks everyone.
[06:18] Sofia: Great — recap: Sofia to send pricing + pilot docs, Ethan to plan the benchmark, security follow-up to cover KMS/SSO/SOC2. We'll aim to start the benchmark the first week of December.
[06:30] [end]
